title: Recursive self-improvement
preview:
Recursive self-improvement (RSI) is a process in which an artificial intelligence (AI) system iteratively designs a more capable successor. This may trigger an intelligence explosion, potentially resulting in the creation of an artificial superintelligence. As of 2026, various RSI-related projects are ongoing and AI companies are increasingly using AI for coding and research, but some human work is still needed and may become a bottleneck.
The development of RSI raises significant ethical and safety concerns, as such systems may evolve in unforeseen ways and could potentially surpass human control or understanding. Unexpected developments in summer 2026 raised new concerns about RSI, leading some top AI firms to acknowledge they may not know how to keep it fully aligned with human values.

== Research ==
In 1950, Alan Turing proposed the idea of developing a "child machine" that would be educated, rather than trying to directly reproduce adult intelligence. Eliezer Yudkowsky coined the concept of "seed AI", an AI capable of improving its own intelligence and which can not only learn new content but also modify its own architecture.
In 2023, the Voyager agent learned to accomplish diverse tasks in Minecraft by iteratively prompting an LLM for code, refining this code based on feedback from the game, and storing the programs that work in an expanding skills library.
In 2024, researchers proposed the framework "STOP" (Self-Taught OPtimiser), in which a "scaffolding" program recursively improves itself using a fixed LLM.
Meta AI has performed various research on the development of large language models capable of self-improvement. This includes their work on "Self-Rewarding Language Models" that studies how to achieve super-human agents that can receive super-human feedback in its training processes.
In May 2025, Google DeepMind unveiled AlphaEvolve, an evolutionary coding agent that uses a LLM to design and optimize algorithms. Starting with an initial algorithm and performance metrics, AlphaEvolve repeatedly mutates or combines existing algorithms using a LLM to generate new candidates, selecting the most promising candidates for further iterations. AlphaEvolve has made several algorithmic discoveries and could be used to optimize components of itself, but a key limitation is the need for automated evaluation functions.
In 2026, many startups started to focus on RSI. AI companies also increasingly delegate the coding and research to LLMs. Anthropic reported that as of May 2026, more than 80% of the code merged into its codebases was generated by its LLM, Claude. The company said however that the time spent reviewing AI-generated code became a new bottleneck.
